title: How to hear this sermon
english: This is a listening version of John Wesley's sermon, The Spirit of Bondage and of Adoption. It is the sermon as printed in John Wesley's 1771 Works. Rendered in modern English.
You have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father.
Romans 8:15.

title: Children by faith
english: Saint Paul here speaks to those who are the children of God by faith. You, he says, who are indeed his children, have drunk into his Spirit. You have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear. But because you are sons, God has sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts (Galatians 4:6). You have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father.

title: Bondage is not adoption
english: The spirit of bondage and fear is widely distant from this loving Spirit of adoption. Those who are influenced only by slavish fear cannot be called the sons of God. Yet some of them may be styled his servants, and are not far from the kingdom of heaven.

title: The greater part
english: But it is to be feared that the bulk of mankind, yes, of what is called the Christian world, have not attained even this. They are still far off, and neither is God in all their thoughts. A few names may be found of those who love God. A few more there are that fear him. But the greater part have neither the fear of God before their eyes, nor the love of God in their hearts.

title: Under the same condemnation
english: Perhaps most of you, who by the mercy of God now partake of a better spirit, may remember the time when you were as they are, when you were under the same condemnation. But at first you did not know it, though you were wallowing daily in your sins and in your blood, until in due time you received the spirit of fear. You received it, for this also is the gift of God. And afterward, fear vanished away, and the Spirit of love filled your hearts.

title: Natural, legal, and under grace
english: One who is in the first state of mind, without fear or love, is in Scripture called a natural man. One who is under the spirit of bondage and fear is sometimes said to be under the law, although that expression more frequently means one who is under the Jewish dispensation, or who thinks himself obliged to observe all the rites and ceremonies of the Jewish law. But one who has exchanged the spirit of fear for the Spirit of love is properly said to be under grace.

Now because it matters greatly to us to know what spirit we are of, I shall endeavor to point out distinctly, first, the state of a natural man, secondly, the state of one who is under the law, and thirdly, the state of one who is under grace.

title: Asleep in the shadow of death
english: And first, the state of a natural man. Scripture represents this as a state of sleep. The voice of God to him is, Awake, you who sleep. For his soul is in a deep sleep. His spiritual senses are not awake. They discern neither spiritual good nor evil. The eyes of his understanding are closed. They are sealed together, and do not see. Clouds and darkness continually rest upon them, for he lies in the valley of the shadow of death.

Hence, having no inlet for the knowledge of spiritual things, all the avenues of his soul being shut up, he is in gross, stupid ignorance of whatever he is most concerned to know. He is utterly ignorant of God, knowing nothing concerning him as he ought to know. He is totally a stranger to the law of God, as to its true, inward, spiritual meaning. He has no conception of that evangelical holiness without which no man shall see the Lord, nor of the happiness which they only find whose life is hid with Christ in God.

title: Secure, because he is blind
english: And for this very reason, because he is fast asleep, he is in some sense at rest. Because he is blind, he is also secure. He says, Tush, no harm shall happen to me. The darkness which covers him on every side keeps him in a kind of peace, so far as peace can consist with the works of the devil, and with an earthly, devilish mind. He does not see that he stands on the edge of the pit. Therefore he does not fear it. He cannot tremble at the danger he does not know. He does not have understanding enough to fear.

Why is it that he is in no dread of God? Because he is totally ignorant of him. If he is not saying in his heart, There is no God, or that he sits on the circle of the heavens and does not humble himself to behold the things which are done on earth, yet he satisfies himself just as well, to all Epicurean intents and purposes, by saying, God is merciful. He confounds and swallows up at once, in that unwieldy idea of mercy, all his holiness and essential hatred of sin, all his justice, wisdom, and truth.

He is in no dread of the vengeance denounced against those who do not obey the blessed law of God, because he does not understand it. He imagines the main point is to do thus, to be outwardly blameless. And he does not see that it extends to every temper, desire, thought, and motion of the heart. Or he fancies that the obligation to this has ceased, that Christ came to destroy the law and the prophets, to save his people in their sins and not from their sins, to bring them to heaven without holiness. This is notwithstanding his own words: Not one jot or tittle of the law shall pass away, till all things are fulfilled. And, Not every one who says to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.

title: Repenting by and by
english: He is secure, because he is utterly ignorant of himself. Hence he talks of repenting by and by. He does not indeed know exactly when, but some time or other before he dies, taking it for granted that this is quite in his own power. For what should hinder his doing it, if he will? If he does but once set a resolution, no fear but he will make it good.

title: Men of learning
english: But this ignorance never glares so strongly as in those who are called men of learning. If a natural man is one of these, he can talk at large of his rational faculties, of the freedom of his will, and of the absolute necessity of such freedom in order to constitute man a moral agent. He reads, and argues, and proves to a demonstration, that every man may do as he will, and may dispose his own heart to evil or good, as it seems best in his own eyes. Thus the God of this world spreads a double veil of blindness over his heart, lest by any means the light of the glorious gospel of Christ should shine upon it.

title: Purple and fine linen
english: From the same ignorance of himself and of God there may sometimes arise, in the natural man, a kind of joy, in congratulating himself upon his own wisdom and goodness. And what the world calls joy he may often possess. He may have pleasure in various kinds, either in gratifying the desires of the flesh, or the desire of the eye, or the pride of life, particularly if he has large possessions, if he enjoys an affluent fortune. Then he may clothe himself in purple and fine linen, and fare sumptuously every day. And so long as he thus does well to himself, men will doubtless speak good of him. They will say, He is a happy man. For indeed this is the sum of worldly happiness: to dress, and visit, and talk, and eat, and drink, and rise up to play.

title: A dream of liberty
english: It is not surprising if one in such circumstances as these, made drowsy with the opiates of flattery and sin, should imagine, among his other waking dreams, that he walks in great liberty. How easily he may persuade himself that he is at liberty from all vulgar errors, and from the prejudice of education, judging exactly right, and keeping clear of all extremes.

I am free, he may say, from all the enthusiasm of weak and narrow souls, from superstition, the disease of fools and cowards, always righteous over much, and from bigotry, which continually falls on those who do not have a free and generous way of thinking. And too sure it is that he is altogether free from the wisdom which comes from above, from holiness, from the religion of the heart, from the whole mind which was in Christ.

title: A willing servant of sin
english: For all this time he is the servant of sin. He commits sin, more or less, day by day. Yet he is not troubled. He is in no bondage, as some speak. He feels no condemnation. He contents himself, even though he should profess to believe that the Christian revelation is of God, with this: Man is frail. We are all weak. Every man has his infirmity.

Perhaps he quotes Scripture. Why, does not Solomon say, The righteous man falls into sin seven times a day? And doubtless they are all hypocrites or enthusiasts who pretend to be better than their neighbors. If at any time a serious thought fixes upon him, he stifles it as soon as possible with, Why should I fear, since God is merciful, and Christ died for sinners? Thus he remains a willing servant of sin, content with the bondage of corruption, inwardly and outwardly unholy, and satisfied with that, not only not conquering sin, but not striving to conquer, particularly that sin which does so easily beset him.

title: Form without power
english: Such is the state of every natural man, whether he is a gross, scandalous transgressor, or a more reputable and decent sinner, having the form, though not the power, of godliness. But how can such a one be convinced of sin? How is he brought to repent? To be under the law? To receive the spirit of bondage to fear? This is the point which is next to be considered.

title: Shaken out of sleep
english: By some awful providence, or by his word applied with the demonstration of his Spirit, God touches the heart of him who lay asleep in darkness and in the shadow of death. He is terribly shaken out of his sleep, and wakes into a consciousness of his danger. Perhaps in a moment, perhaps by degrees, the eyes of his understanding are opened, and now first, the veil being in part removed, discern the real state he is in. Horrid light breaks in upon his soul, such light as may be conceived to gleam from the bottomless pit, from the lowest deep, from a lake of fire burning with brimstone.

He at last sees that the loving, the merciful God is also a consuming fire, that he is a just God and a terrible one, rendering to every man according to his works, entering into judgment with the ungodly for every idle word, yes, and for the imaginations of the heart. He now clearly perceives that the great and holy God is of purer eyes than to behold iniquity, that he is an avenger of every one who rebels against him, and repays the wicked to his face, and that it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.

title: The commandment is exceedingly broad
english: The inward, spiritual meaning of the law of God now begins to glare upon him. He perceives the commandment is exceedingly broad, and there is nothing hidden from the light of it. He is convinced that every part of it relates not merely to outward sin or obedience, but to what passes in the secret recesses of the soul, which no eye but God's can penetrate.

If he now hears, You shall not kill, God speaks in thunder, He who hates his brother is a murderer. He who says to his brother, You fool, is in danger of hell-fire. If the law says, You shall not commit adultery, the voice of the Lord sounds in his ears, He who looks on a woman to lust after her has committed adultery with her already in his heart. And thus, in every point, he feels the word of God quick and powerful, sharper than a two-edged sword. It pierces even to the dividing asunder of his soul and spirit, his joints and marrow. And so much the more, because he is conscious to himself of having neglected so great a salvation, of having trodden under foot the Son of God, who would have saved him from his sins, and of having counted the blood of the covenant an unholy thing, a common, unsanctifying thing.

title: Cleft open
english: And as he knows all things are naked and opened to the eyes of him with whom we have to do, so he sees himself naked, stripped of all the fig leaves which he had sewn together, of all his poor pretenses to religion or virtue, and of his wretched excuses for sinning against God.

He now sees himself like the ancient sacrifices, cleft in two, as it were, from the neck downward, so that all within him stands confessed. His heart is bare, and he sees it is all sin, deceitful above all things, desperately wicked, that it is altogether corrupt and abominable, more than it is possible for tongue to express, that there dwells in it no good thing, but unrighteousness and ungodliness only, every motion of it, every temper and thought, being only evil continually.

title: The second death
english: And he not only sees, but feels in himself, by an emotion of soul which he cannot describe, that for the sins of his heart, were his life without blame, which yet it is not, and cannot be, seeing an evil tree cannot bring forth good fruit, he deserves to be cast into the fire that never shall be quenched. He feels that the wages, the just reward of sin, of his sin above all, is death, even the second death, the death which does not die, the destruction of body and soul in hell.

title: The dream ends
english: Here ends his pleasing dream, his delusive rest, his false peace, his vain security. His joy now vanishes as a cloud. Pleasures once loved delight no more. They pall upon the taste. He loathes the nauseous sweet. He is weary of bearing them. The shadows of happiness flee away, and sink into oblivion. So that he is stripped of all, and wanders to and fro, seeking rest, but finding none.

title: A wounded spirit
english: The fumes of those opiates being now dispelled, he feels the anguish of a wounded spirit. He finds that sin let loose upon the soul, whether it is pride, anger, or evil desire, whether self-will, malice, envy, revenge, or any other, is perfect misery. He feels sorrow of heart for the blessings he has lost, and the curse which has come upon him, and remorse for having thus destroyed himself and despised his own mercies. He feels fear, from a lively sense of the wrath of God, and of the consequences of his wrath, of the punishment which he has justly deserved, and which he sees hanging over his head. He feels fear of death, as being to him the gate of hell, the entrance of death eternal. He feels fear of the devil, the executioner of the wrath and righteous vengeance of God. He feels fear of men, who, if they were able to kill his body, would thereby plunge both body and soul into hell. He feels fear sometimes rising to such a height that the poor, sinful, guilty soul is terrified with everything, with nothing, with shades, with a leaf shaken by the wind.

Yes, sometimes it may even border upon distraction, making a man drunk, though not with wine, suspending the exercise of the memory, of the understanding, of all the natural faculties. Sometimes it may approach to the very brink of despair, so that he who trembles at the name of death may yet be ready to plunge into it every moment, to choose strangling rather than life. Well may such a man roar, like him of old, for the very disquiet of his heart. Well may he cry out, The spirit of a man may sustain his infirmities, but a wounded spirit who can bear?

title: Free only to evil
english: Now he truly desires to break loose from sin, and begins to struggle with it. But though he strives with all his might, he cannot conquer. Sin is mightier than he. He would gladly escape, but he is so fast in prison that he cannot get forth. He resolves against sin, but yet sins on. He sees the snare, and abhors it, and runs into it. So much does his boasted reason avail. Only to enhance his guilt, and increase his misery. Such is the freedom of his will. Free only to evil. Free to drink in iniquity like water, to wander farther and farther from the living God, and to do more despite to the Spirit of grace.

title: The chain he cannot break
english: The more he strives, wishes, and labors to be free, the more he feels his chains, the grievous chains of sin, wherewith Satan binds him and leads him captive at his will. His servant he is, though he complains ever so much. Though he rebels, he cannot prevail. He is still in bondage and fear, by reason of sin. Generally, of some outward sin to which he is peculiarly disposed, either by nature, custom, or outward circumstances. But always, of some inward sin, some evil temper or unholy affection. And the more he frets against it, the more it prevails. He may bite, but cannot break his chain. Thus he toils without end, repenting and sinning, and repenting and sinning again, until at length the poor, sinful, helpless wretch is even at his wit's end, and can barely groan, O wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?

title: The apostle's portrait
english: This whole struggle of one who is under the law, under the spirit of fear and bondage, is beautifully described by the apostle in the foregoing chapter, speaking in the person of an awakened man.

I, he says, was alive without the law once. Romans 7:9. I had much life, wisdom, strength, and virtue, so I thought. But when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died. When the commandment, in its spiritual meaning, came to my heart, with the power of God, my inbred sin was stirred up, fretted, inflamed, and all my virtue died away.

And the commandment, which was ordained to life, I found to be to death. For sin, taking occasion by the commandment, deceived me, and by it slew me. Romans 7:10-11. It came upon me unawares, slew all my hopes, and plainly showed, in the midst of life I was in death.

Wherefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good. Romans 7:12. I no longer lay the blame on this, but on the corruption of my own heart. I acknowledge that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin. Romans 7:14. I now see both the spiritual nature of the law, and my own carnal, devilish heart, sold under sin, totally enslaved, like slaves bought with money, who were absolutely at their master's disposal.

For that which I do, I allow not. For what I would, I do not, but what I hate, that I do. Romans 7:15. Such is the bondage under which I groan, such the tyranny of my hard master. To will is present with me, but how to perform that which is good, I do not find. For the good that I would, I do not, but the evil which I would not, that I do. Romans 7:18-19.

I find a law, an inward constraining power, that when I would do good, evil is present with me. For I delight in, or consent to, the law of God, after the inward man. Romans 7:21-22. In my mind: so the apostle explains himself in the words that immediately follow, and so the inward man is understood in all other Greek writers.

But I see another law in my members, another constraining power, warring against the law of my mind, or inward man, and bringing me into captivity to the law, or power, of sin. Romans 7:23. It drags me, as it were, at my conqueror's chariot wheels, into the very thing which my soul abhors.

O wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death? Romans 7:24. Who shall deliver me from this helpless, dying life, from this bondage of sin and misery? Until this is done, I myself, or rather that I, the man I am now personating, with the mind, or inward man, serve the law of God. My mind, my conscience, is on God's side. But with the flesh, with my body, I serve the law of sin. Romans 7:25. I am hurried away by a force I cannot resist.

title: Who shall deliver me
english: How lively a portrait this is of one under the law. One who feels the burden he cannot shake off, who pants after liberty, power, and love, but is in fear and bondage still, until the time that God answers the wretched man, crying out, Who shall deliver me from this bondage of sin, from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ your Lord.

title: No longer under the law
english: Then it is that this miserable bondage ends, and he is no more under the law, but under grace. This state we are, thirdly, to consider: the state of one who has found grace, or favor, in the sight of God, even the Father, and who has the grace, or power, of the Holy Ghost, reigning in his heart, who has received, in the language of the apostle, the Spirit of adoption, whereby he now cries, Abba, Father.

title: All my goodness
english: He cried to the Lord in his trouble, and God delivers him out of his distress. His eyes are opened in quite another manner than before, even to see a loving, gracious God. While he is calling, I beseech you, show me your glory, he hears a voice in his inmost soul, I will make all my goodness pass before you, and I will proclaim the name of the Lord. I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and I will show mercy to whom I will show mercy.

And it is not long before the Lord descends in the cloud, and proclaims the name of the Lord. Then he sees, but not with eyes of flesh and blood, The Lord, the Lord God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth, keeping mercy for thousands, and forgiving iniquities and transgression and sin.

title: The light of his pardoning love
english: Heavenly, healing light now breaks in upon his soul. He looks on him whom he had pierced, and God, who out of darkness commanded light to shine, shines in his heart. He sees the light of the glorious love of God, in the face of Jesus Christ. He has a divine evidence of things not seen by sense, even of the deep things of God, more particularly of the love of God, of his pardoning love to him who believes in Jesus.

Overpowered with the sight, his whole soul cries out, My Lord and my God. For he sees all his iniquities laid on him who bore them in his own body on the tree. He beholds the Lamb of God taking away his sins. How clearly now he discerns that God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, making him sin for us who knew no sin, that we might be made the righteousness of God through him. And that he himself is reconciled to God, by that blood of the covenant.

title: Bondage to fear ends
english: Here end both the guilt and the power of sin. He can now say, I am crucified with Christ. Nevertheless I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me. And the life which I now live in the flesh, even in this mortal body, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.

Here end remorse, and sorrow of heart, and the anguish of a wounded spirit. God turns his heaviness into joy. He made sore, and now his hands bind up. Here ends also that bondage to fear, for his heart stands fast, believing in the Lord. He cannot fear any longer the wrath of God, for he knows it is now turned away from him, and he looks upon him no more as an angry judge, but as a loving Father. He cannot fear the devil, knowing he has no power, except it is given him from above. He fears not hell, being an heir of the kingdom of heaven. Consequently, he has no fear of death, by reason of which he was, in time past, for so many years, subject to bondage.

Rather, knowing that if the earthly house of this tabernacle is dissolved, he has a building of God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. He groans earnestly, desiring to be clothed upon with that house which is from heaven. He groans to shake off this house of earth, that mortality may be swallowed up of life, knowing that God has wrought him for the selfsame thing, who has also given him the earnest of his Spirit.

title: Free from sin
english: And where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. Liberty not only from guilt and fear, but from sin, from that heaviest of all yokes, that basest of all bondage. His labor is not now in vain. The snare is broken, and he is delivered. He not only strives, but likewise prevails. He not only fights, but conquers also.

Henceforth he does not serve sin. Romans 6:6ff. He is dead to sin, and alive to God. Sin does not now reign, even in his mortal body, nor does he obey it in the desires of it. He does not yield his members as instruments of unrighteousness to sin, but as instruments of righteousness to God. For being now made free from sin, he has become the servant of righteousness.

title: We cry, Abba, Father
english: Thus, having peace with God, through our Lord Jesus Christ, rejoicing in hope of the glory of God, and having power over all sin, over every evil desire, and temper, and word, and work, he is a living witness of the glorious liberty of the sons of God. All of them, being partakers of like precious faith, bear record with one voice, We have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father.

title: Love shed abroad
english: It is this Spirit which continually works in them, both to will and to do of his good pleasure. It is he who sheds the love of God abroad in their hearts, and the love of all mankind, thereby purifying their hearts from the love of the world, from the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eye, and the pride of life. It is by him they are delivered from anger and pride, from all vile and inordinate affections. In consequence, they are delivered from evil words and works, from all unholiness of conversation, doing no evil to any child of man, and being zealous of all good works.

title: Three states, side by side
english: To sum up all. The natural man neither fears nor loves God. One under the law fears. One under grace loves him. The first has no light in the things of God, but walks in utter darkness. The second sees the painful light of hell. The third, the joyous light of heaven. He who sleeps in death has a false peace. He who is awakened has no peace at all. He who believes has true peace, the peace of God filling and ruling his heart.

The heathen, baptized or unbaptized, has a fancied liberty, which is indeed licentiousness. The Jew, or one under the Jewish dispensation, is in heavy, grievous bondage. The Christian enjoys the true glorious liberty of the sons of God. An unawakened child of the devil sins willingly. One who is awakened sins unwillingly. A child of God does not sin, but keeps himself, and the wicked one does not touch him.

To conclude: the natural man neither conquers nor fights. The man under the law fights with sin, but cannot conquer. The man under grace fights and conquers, yes, is more than conqueror, through him who loves him.

title: Sincere is not enough
english: From this plain account of the threefold state of man, the natural, the legal, and the evangelical, it appears that it is not sufficient to divide mankind into sincere and insincere. A man may be sincere in any of these states, not only when he has the Spirit of adoption, but while he has the spirit of bondage to fear. Yes, while he has neither this fear, nor love. For undoubtedly there may be sincere heathens, as well as sincere Jews or Christians. This circumstance, then, does by no means prove that a man is in a state of acceptance with God.

title: Examine yourselves
english: Examine yourselves, therefore, not only whether you are sincere, but whether you are in the faith. Examine narrowly, for it matters much to you. What is the ruling principle in your soul? Is it the love of God? Is it the fear of God? Or is it neither one nor the other? Is it not rather the love of the world? The love of pleasure, or gain, of ease, or reputation? If so, you have not come so far as a Jew. You are but a heathen still.

Have you heaven in your heart? Have you the Spirit of adoption, ever crying, Abba, Father? Or do you cry to God, as out of the belly of hell, overwhelmed with sorrow and fear? Or are you a stranger to this whole affair, and cannot imagine what I mean? Heathen, pull off the mask. You have never put on Christ. Stand barefaced. Look up to heaven, and own, before him who lives forever and ever, that you have no part, either among the sons or among the servants of God.

title: Of the devil
english: Whoever you are, do you commit sin, or do you not? If you do, is it willingly or unwillingly? In either case, God has told you whose you are: He who commits sin is of the devil. If you commit it willingly, you are his faithful servant. He will not fail to reward your labor. If unwillingly, still you are his servant. God deliver you out of his hands.

title: Fighting, or at ease
english: Are you daily fighting against all sin, and daily more than conqueror? I acknowledge you for a child of God. O stand fast in your glorious liberty. Are you fighting, but not conquering, striving for the mastery, but not able to attain? Then you are not yet a believer in Christ. But follow on, and you shall know the Lord. Are you not fighting at all, but leading an easy, indolent, fashionable life? O how have you dared to name the name of Christ, only to make it a reproach among the heathen? Awake, you sleeper. Call upon your God, before the deep swallows you up.

title: Fear mixed with sleep
english: Perhaps one reason why so many think of themselves more highly than they ought to think, why they do not discern what state they are in, is that these several states of soul are often mingled together, and in some measure meet in one and the same person.

Thus experience shows that the legal state, or state of fear, is frequently mixed with the natural. For few men are so fast asleep in sin, but they are sometimes more or less awakened. As the Spirit of God does not wait for the call of man, so at some times he will be heard. He puts them in fear, so that for a season, at least, the heathen know themselves to be but men. They feel the burden of sin, and earnestly desire to flee from the wrath to come. But not long. They seldom suffer the arrows of conviction to go deep into their souls, but quickly stifle the grace of God, and return to their wallowing in the mire.

title: A dawning, still far off
english: In the same manner, the evangelical state, or state of love, is frequently mixed with the legal. For few of those who have the spirit of bondage and fear remain always without hope. The wise and gracious God rarely suffers this, for he remembers that we are but dust. And he does not will that the flesh should fail before him, or the spirit which he has made. Therefore, at such times as he sees good, he gives a dawning of light to them who sit in darkness. He causes a part of his goodness to pass before them, and shows he is a God who hears prayer. They see the promise which is by faith in Christ Jesus, though it is yet far off, and hereby they are encouraged to run with patience the race which is set before them.

title: How far a natural man may go
english: Another reason why many deceive themselves is that they do not consider how far a man may go, and yet be in a natural, or at best a legal, state. A man may be of a compassionate and a benevolent temper. He may be affable, courteous, generous, friendly. He may have some degree of meekness, patience, temperance, and of many other moral virtues. He may feel many desires of shaking off all vice, and of attaining higher degrees of virtue. He may abstain from much evil, perhaps from all that is grossly contrary to justice, mercy, or truth. He may do much good, may feed the hungry, clothe the naked, and relieve the widow and fatherless. He may attend public worship, use prayer in private, and read many books of devotion. And yet for all this he may be a mere natural man, knowing neither himself nor God, equally a stranger to the Spirit of fear and to that of love, having neither repented nor believed the gospel.

title: Not adoption yet
english: But suppose there were added to all this a deep conviction of sin, with much fear of the wrath of God, vehement desires to cast off every sin, and to fulfill all righteousness, frequent rejoicing in hope, and touches of love often glancing upon the soul. Yet neither do these prove a man to be under grace, to have true, living, Christian faith, unless the Spirit of adoption abides in his heart, unless he can continually cry, Abba, Father.

title: Not called to tremble
english: Beware, then, you who are called by the name of Christ, that you come not short of the mark of your high calling. Beware you rest not, either in a natural state, with too many who are accounted good Christians, or in a legal state, wherein those who are highly esteemed of men are generally content to live and die.

Nay, but God has prepared better things for you, if you follow on till you attain. You are not called to fear and tremble like devils, but to rejoice and love, like the angels of God. You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength. You shall rejoice evermore. You shall pray without ceasing. You shall in everything give thanks. You shall do the will of God on earth, as it is done in heaven.

O prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect will of God. Now present yourself a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God. Where you have already attained, hold fast, and by reaching forth to those things which are before, press on, until the God of peace makes you perfect in every good work, working in you that which is well-pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
